R02-C-01: Boredom is usually described as a kind of emptiness, the feeling of having nothing to feel. On this view it is a residue, what remains when interest drains away, and the natural response is to fill the space with whatever is at hand, much as one might fill an awkward silence with remarks about the weather. The description is understandable, since boredom rarely announces any object of its own, but it gets the state almost exactly backwards. Boredom is not an absence. It is an active and often insistent signal that the activity in front of us is failing to engage the capacities we have available, and it exists to make us do something about that. The comparison with other unpleasant states is instructive. Hunger is disagreeable, but nobody concludes from this that hunger is a defect; its discomfort is the means by which it gets us to eat. Boredom works in a similar way. A person bored by a repetitive clerical task does not merely register that the task is dull; she feels restless, glances at the clock, begins to imagine alternatives. The unpleasantness is doing work. It pushes attention away from a situation that offers too little and towards a search for one that offers more, whether that means a harder problem, a different companion or simply a walk. None of this implies that boredom is always benign. A signal is useful only when there is some way to act on it, and many situations offer none. The patient in a waiting room, the passenger on a delayed train and the worker who cannot leave a monotonous post all receive the message without being able to respond, and in such cases boredom curdles into frustration or something close to despair. There are also signs that people will sometimes reach for almost any stimulation rather than endure an unoccupied mind, even stimulation they would otherwise find unpleasant. The signal, in other words, can be loud enough to drive choices that serve no one, and a theory of boredom that celebrated it without reservation would be as misleading as one that dismissed it. What follows is a reason to be wary of the most popular remedy. If boredom is a message about the fit between a person and an activity, then an endless supply of small distractions does not answer the message; it merely muffles it. Someone who reaches for a screen at every lull may never feel bored for long, but may also never learn what the boredom was pointing at: a job that has stopped stretching them, a routine that has outlived its purpose, a curiosity that has gone unfed. The more useful question, when boredom arrives, is not how to make it stop but what it is about.
R02-C-02: Popular advice about habits tends to treat them as a contest of will. Bad habits persist, on this account, because people lack the resolve to stop, and good ones fail to form because people give up too soon. The remedy is accordingly motivational: set firmer goals, remind yourself why they matter, and try harder. This view has the appeal of moral simplicity, since it locates every failure in a lack of character and every success in effort, and it is repeated in a great deal of well-meant advice. The trouble with this picture is that it misdescribes what a habit is. A habit is not a desire that has grown strong but a response that has become attached to a context, so that the context itself, rather than any present intention, sets the behaviour going. Consider someone who checks her phone each time she sits down on the morning train. At first the action may have been chosen, perhaps as a way of passing an otherwise idle part of the trip, but after hundreds of repetitions it no longer needs choosing. The seat, the motion of the carriage and the familiar stretch of the journey are enough to bring the hand to the pocket, and she may find the phone in her hand before she has formed any wish to look at it. Asking her to resolve more firmly misses the point, since resolve is not what produces the act. The cue is. If this is right, the most effective way to change a habit is often to change the circumstances that trigger it, not to strengthen the will that opposes it. Putting the phone in a bag rather than a pocket, sitting in a different carriage, or giving the first minutes of the journey to some specific task all interrupt the link between cue and response. Each of these requires a single decision rather than a renewed act of resistance every morning, which is precisely why such changes tend to outlast good intentions. It is often observed that people find it easier to alter their routines after moving house or changing jobs, and the account explains why: the old cues have simply disappeared, and with them much of the pressure to repeat old behaviour. Two cautions are in order, however, if the argument is not to be pushed further than it can go. First, not every repeated behaviour is a habit in this sense; some acts are repeated because the person goes on wanting the result each time, and for these, motivation does matter. Second, the power of context cuts both ways. The same disruption that frees someone from an unwanted routine can dissolve a welcome one, which is why a regular exercise habit so often lapses after a move. Willpower is not irrelevant, then, but it is a poor tool for a job that the environment, suitably arranged, performs more cheaply and more reliably.
R02-C-03: Few findings in happiness research have travelled further than the idea of hedonic adaptation. People who experience a good or bad change in their circumstances, the finding goes, tend over time to drift back towards their earlier level of wellbeing, as though each of us were tethered to a personal set point from which events can pull us only temporarily. In its popular form the idea has hardened into something like a philosophy: since we adapt to everything, the pursuit of better circumstances is futile, and contentment is a matter of temperament rather than of how one lives. The research, read with any care, gives considerably less support to this conclusion than its popularity would suggest. To begin with, adaptation is uneven. People appear to adjust quite quickly to many gains, such as a higher salary or a larger house, which soon become the new normal against which further comparisons are made. But some conditions resist adaptation stubbornly. Persistent noise, a long and unpredictable commute and chronic pain seem to remain unpleasant year after year, perhaps because they keep demanding attention and never settle into the background of experience. The lesson is not that circumstances do not matter but that they matter selectively: what we stop noticing stops affecting us, and what keeps intruding does not. A second problem lies in how the evidence is summarised. Many studies report that, on average, a group's wellbeing returns towards its earlier level some time after an event such as marriage or the loss of a job. An average, however, can conceal very different individual paths. A group in which some people end up much happier and others much less happy can show almost no change overall, and the reassuring flat line then describes almost nobody in it. When researchers have examined individuals rather than averages, they have tended to find that a substantial minority do not return to where they began, which is precisely the information that a headline about set points discards. None of this means that the original insight was mistaken. People do adapt to a great deal, and the observation usefully corrects the belief that one more purchase or promotion will produce lasting delight. The error lies in the step from 'we adapt to much' to 'nothing we do makes a lasting difference'. That step is no more justified than its opposite, and it carries a practical cost, since it can discourage people from changing the very conditions, the noisy flat or the gruelling journey, that are most likely to keep wearing them down.
R02-C-04: One influential account of curiosity holds that it arises from a gap between what a person already knows and what that person would like to know. On this view curiosity is not a general appetite for novelty but a response to a specific, noticed absence: the missing end of a story, the answer to a riddle, the identity of the person who has just telephoned. The account has much to recommend it. It explains why we are rarely curious about subjects of which we know nothing, since we cannot notice a gap in a field we cannot see, and why a little knowledge is often more stimulating than none. It also explains why curiosity so frequently vanishes the moment the answer arrives, leaving behind a satisfaction that is oddly short-lived. Yet the information gap account fits some cases far better than others. It is at its strongest when the gap is well defined, as in a puzzle with a single solution or a mystery with a culprit. It is weaker when applied to the kind of curiosity that drifts without a target, the impulse that leads someone to wander along the shelves of a library, to turn over stones on a beach or to follow a footnote simply to see where it leads. In these cases there is no specific question waiting to be answered. If anything, the person seeks out situations in which questions might arise, and the pleasure lies as much in the searching as in any particular discovery. Defenders of the account sometimes reply that the wanderer is simply responding to many small gaps in quick succession. The reply preserves the theory, but at a cost. If any movement of attention whatever can be redescribed after the fact as the closing of a gap, the account no longer explains anything in particular; it becomes a vocabulary rather than a hypothesis. It seems more accurate to say that there are at least two kinds of curiosity, one that seeks to close a specific gap and one that seeks to encounter the unfamiliar, and that the influential account is a good theory of the first. The distinction matters for anyone who wishes to cultivate curiosity, and for teachers above all. A lesson built on the first kind poses a sharp question and withholds the answer just long enough to make it wanted. A lesson built on the second provides a rich environment and the time to wander in it, without specifying in advance what ought to be found. Both have their place, but a classroom organised entirely around the first may produce students who are excellent at finishing puzzles and rather less inclined to go looking for them.
R02-C-05: Ask people what grief involves and many will describe a sequence: denial, then anger, then bargaining, then depression, and at last acceptance. The sequence has become so familiar that it can seem like a discovery about human nature, as settled as the stages of a fever. It began, however, as a description of how some terminally ill patients responded to the news of their own approaching death, drawn from clinical conversations rather than from any systematic study of the bereaved. Its migration from the dying to the grieving, and from a set of observations to something closer to a timetable, happened largely outside the kind of research that might have tested it. When grief has been studied directly, the tidy sequence has not fared well. Bereaved people commonly report several of the named feelings at once, or in no particular order, and many report some of them hardly at all. Perhaps the most striking finding is how many people cope with a loss far better than the model would lead one to expect, experiencing intense sorrow that gradually eases over months without passing through anything resembling distinct stages. Resilience of this kind is not denial in disguise; for a good number of people it seems simply to be the ordinary course that grief takes. The harm of the model lies less in its inaccuracy than in what people do with it. A description of what some people feel becomes a standard of what everyone ought to feel, and departures from the standard begin to look like problems requiring attention. The widow who is not angry may be told that she has not yet faced her loss; the son who feels relief after a parent's long illness may wonder what is wrong with him. Friends, and even professionals, may wait for a stage that never arrives, or press a grieving person to move on to the next one as though grief were a course with a syllabus. It would be unfair, though, to treat the model's popularity as mere credulity. It arrived at a time when dying and grief were seldom spoken of openly, and it gave people words for feelings, anger above all, that they might otherwise have hidden or been ashamed of. That was a real service, and it should not be forgotten in the rush to correct the record. The task now is to keep what the model offered, the permission to feel a wide range of things, while dropping the suggestion that those feelings must arrive in a fixed order, or arrive at all.
R02-C-06: It has become a commonplace that rewarding people for doing what they already enjoy can make them enjoy it less. Picture a child who draws for the pleasure of it and is then promised a prize for each picture. While the prizes continue, the drawing may increase. When they stop, the child may draw less than before the prizes began, as though the activity had been converted from play into work and then left unpaid. The phenomenon is real, and it has been reproduced often enough to deserve to be taken seriously. What is less often noticed is how many conditions it depends upon, and how quickly it fades when they are absent. The effect appears most reliably when the reward is tangible, expected in advance and given for doing the task rather than for doing it well. A prize announced beforehand and handed over for every picture invites the child to understand the drawing as a means to the prize. An unexpected treat, by contrast, cannot have been the reason for drawing, and praise that tells the child something about the quality of the work may even strengthen interest, since it feeds the sense of competence that made the activity enjoyable in the first place. The same physical reward can therefore have opposite effects depending on what it communicates to the person who receives it. Equally important, the effect presupposes that there was interest to undermine. Many tasks that people are paid or rewarded for, from sorting files to practising scales, hold little intrinsic appeal at the outset, and for these, rewards cannot crowd out an enjoyment that was never there. Indeed, a reward may keep someone at a dull task long enough for skill to grow and for the task itself to become absorbing, so that interest arrives because of the incentive rather than in spite of it. The sensible conclusion lies between two slogans. Those who say that rewards destroy motivation generalise from a narrow set of conditions; those who say that people simply do whatever they are paid to do ignore the conditions entirely. The better question in any particular case is how the reward is likely to be read: as an attempt to control behaviour that would otherwise not occur, or as information about how well something is being done. The first reading tends to erode interest in activities that people already value; the second tends to support it.
R02-C-07: The word 'stress' entered the study of living things from the study of materials, where its meaning is reasonably exact: the internal force per unit area within a body subjected to a load. In engineering, stress is distinguished from strain, the deformation that the load produces, and both are distinguished from the load itself. When the word was borrowed to describe what happens to organisms under pressure, these distinctions did not travel with it. In ordinary speech, and in a good deal of research, 'stress' can refer to the demanding situation, to the bodily and emotional reaction it provokes, or to the relation between the two, and it is often far from clear which of these is meant. A survey announcing that most workers feel stressed may be measuring their workloads, their symptoms or their sense of being overwhelmed, and the headline rarely says which. The slippage is not merely a matter of untidy usage. Consider the familiar claim that stress is bad for health. If stress means the reaction, and the reaction is defined partly by its harmful effects, the claim is close to true by definition. If stress means the demanding situation, the claim is plainly false as a generalisation, since many people meet heavy demands without harm and some appear to thrive on them. Only if stress means a particular relation, demands that exceed what a person believes they can manage, does the claim become a substantive hypothesis that could turn out to be wrong. Much popular discussion moves among these meanings without noticing, and so acquires the authority of the first reading and the scope of the second. The same confusion shadows the more recent enthusiasm for 'good stress'. To say that some stress is beneficial may mean that some demanding situations are worth seeking out, which is uncontroversial; or that some physiological reactions to demand improve performance, which is plausible within limits; or that people who interpret their reactions as helpful fare better than those who do not, which is a specific claim requiring specific evidence. Advice built on the phrase often slides from the first meaning, which everyone accepts, to the third, which is the one actually being sold. Each of the three deserves to be judged on its own evidence, and the plausibility of the first lends nothing to the third. It might seem that the remedy is to abandon the word altogether. That would be a mistake, and not only because ordinary language is not so easily reformed. The very breadth of the term has allowed researchers in physiology, psychology, sociology and medicine to recognise that they were studying related things, and it has drawn attention to connections, between working conditions and heart disease, say, that narrower vocabularies might have kept apart. Whole programmes of research, on bereavement, on unemployment, on the burdens of caring for a sick relative, found a common frame in it. A concept can be scientifically fruitful precisely because it is loose at the edges, so long as those who use it know where the looseness lies. What the word cannot do is carry an argument by itself. The useful discipline is to ask, whenever a claim about stress is made, which of its meanings is in play, and whether the evidence offered supports the claim under that meaning or only under a different one. A finding about reactions does not automatically license advice about situations, and a finding about interpretations says little about either. Keeping the senses apart costs a few extra words; failing to keep them apart has cost a good deal of confusion, some of it in the very places where clarity matters most.
R02-C-08: For a time it seemed that psychology had found the mechanism of willpower. Self-control, the theory held, draws on a limited resource that is used up by effort and replenished by rest. Resisting a tempting food, suppressing an emotion or forcing oneself through a tedious task would each deplete the same store, leaving a person less able to exercise control on whatever came next. The idea had the great advantage of matching experience. Most of us know the evening collapse that follows a day of holding ourselves together, and the theory seemed to explain it with all the economy of a fuel gauge. It also seemed to account for a scattering of everyday puzzles: why a dieter might lapse late in the day rather than at breakfast, why hard decisions get put off until morning, why a quarrel flares more easily after a draining afternoon. The theory has fared badly under closer scrutiny. Large coordinated attempts to reproduce the basic effect, in which many laboratories ran the same procedure, found it to be far smaller than early reports had suggested and in some cases close to nothing. A particularly vivid version of the theory, which identified the resource with blood sugar and held that a sweet drink could restore flagging self-control, met an additional difficulty: effortful thinking appears to change the brain's overall energy consumption only slightly, far too little for the proposed mechanism to work as described. Some studies also reported that people who believed willpower to be plentiful showed little or no depletion, a result awkward for any theory in which the resource is a physical quantity. Yet it does not follow that the experience the theory set out to explain is an illusion. People do grow less willing to persist after sustained effort, and that change deserves an account. A more promising one treats the feeling of mental fatigue not as a reading on an emptying tank but as a signal about priorities. On this view, continued effort on one task carries an opportunity cost, the value of everything else one might be doing instead, and the sense of weariness rises as that cost accumulates, nudging attention away from obligation and towards rest, pleasure or novelty. What looks like running out is better described as a shift in what the mind is willing to pay for. The difference between the two pictures is not merely academic. If willpower is a fuel, the sensible strategy is rationing: avoid unnecessary decisions, save strength for what matters, and accept failure when the tank is low. If fatigue is a signal about value, the strategy changes. Tasks that feel meaningful or rewarding should be less draining than equally demanding tasks that do not, and changing how a task is framed, or what it leads to, may restore persistence where rest alone would not. The second picture does not make self-control easy, but it relocates the problem from the size of a store to the weighing of competing goods. It also suggests why the same evening can feel exhausting at a desk and effortless at a hobby, though the demands on attention may be much the same. The episode also carries a lesson about how attractive ideas spread. The resource model was simple, intuitive and flattering to common experience, and these virtues helped it travel far beyond the evidence that supported it. None of this required anyone to be careless or dishonest; it is simply how persuasive ideas tend to behave. Its decline is not a refutation of everyday wisdom about tiredness; it is a reminder that a vivid metaphor can capture a real phenomenon while getting its mechanism entirely wrong.
